How Capitalism Produces Political Backlash

Stephen Weymouth

Dean’s Professor

2026-11-09

On September 15, 2008, Lehman Brothers filed the largest bankruptcy in U.S. history. Within weeks governments were rescuing the banks.

Timing: 0–3 minutes.

  • Lehman listed $639 billion in assets and $613 billion in debts (History.com). U.S. unemployment rose from 5.0 percent in December 2007 to 10.0 percent in October 2009 (BLS).
  • On November 4: decline became political through places. Today opens with a puzzle (the next two slides) and Wolf’s answer: the financial crisis and the rescue that followed.
  • Photograph: reporters outside Lehman Brothers’ headquarters in Midtown Manhattan on the night of September 15, 2008.

[Sources] - Martin Wolf, The Crisis of Democratic Capitalism (2023), ch. 4, pp. 99–110. History.com, “Lehman Brothers collapses” (updated May 28, 2025); BLS, “The Recession of 2007–2009,” February 2012. Background photograph: Robert Scoble, Lehman Brothers headquarters, September 15, 2008, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0, resized.

Capitalism’s image has slipped in the U.S.

Gallup, Socialism’s Positive Rating Tops 40% for First Time, September 2026.

Small business still has a 95 percent positive rating, while big business has fallen to 35 percent.

Why would people in the world’s largest market economy think less of capitalism?

Timing: 3–6 minutes. Pose the key-line as the session’s puzzle and do not answer it yet; Wolf’s chapter is the answer.

  • Chart, percent positive (Gallup): capitalism 61 (2010), 61 (2012), 60 (2016), 56 (2018), 60 (2019), 60 (2021), 54 (2025, the series low), 55 (2026); socialism 36, 39, 35, 37, 39, 38, 39, 43 (2026, the series high and the first reading above 40).
  • Same survey, 2010 to 2026: big business 49 to 35, free enterprise 86 to 77, small business 95 to 95.
  • Survey: August 3–24, 2026, 1,200 adults by telephone, margin of error plus or minus 4 points. Gallup first asked in 2010, two years after the crisis, so there is no pre-crisis reading.

[Sources] - Gallup, Lydia Saad, September 23, 2026; Gallup, September 8, 2025; series in instructor/2026-11-09-series.json; original drawing.

Young adults now rate socialism above capitalism

Among adults under 30, capitalism’s positive rating fell from 68 percent in 2010 to 45 percent in 2018.

Democrats’ rating of capitalism fell from 51 to 35 percent, while Republicans’ rose.

Today’s young adults grew up during the crisis or the slow recovery that followed it.

Gallup, Socialism’s Positive Rating Tops 40% for First Time, September 2026.

Timing: 6–9 minutes. Ask what “socialism” means to someone who was ten years old in 2008; take two answers, then move on.

  • Chart, 2026, percent positive, capitalism and socialism: ages 18–34, 43 and 57; 35–54, 50 and 45; 55 and older, 65 and 34. Gallup changed its age groups, so the 2026 groups do not match 2010’s.
  • Ages 18–29: capitalism 68 (2010) and 45 (2018); socialism 51 in both years (Gallup, August 13, 2018).
  • By party, capitalism positive (party identifiers without leaners): Republicans 71 (2010) and 75 (2026); independents 61 and 56; Democrats 51 and 35. Democrats’ socialism rating: 50 and 65. The 2026 rise in socialism’s rating came entirely from independents (Gallup).
  • Keep the discussion on what the words mean to respondents and why views moved; do not ask students their own views or party.

[Sources] - Gallup, September 23, 2026; Gallup, Frank Newport, August 13, 2018; series in instructor/2026-11-09-series.json; original drawing.

Your IB Voice

The crisis and capitalism

Positive views of capitalism in the U.S. have slipped since 2010, most among the young. Using one piece of evidence from Wolf, explain how the 2008 financial crisis could have changed the way people judge capitalism and those who run it.

10 minutes · Individual · Notes permitted

Timing: 9–19 minutes. Leave the prompt up for the full ten minutes. Do not preview the hypotheses.

  • Passages students will reach for: households with flat or falling incomes (p. 102); the rescue of “both banks and bankers” while families lost homes (p. 104); the crisis made failures visible and “clearly the fault of certain specific elite institutions and people” (p. 109).

[Sources] - Wolf (2023), pp. 102, 104, 109.

Competing explanations

Why did so many people turn against capitalism’s leaders after 2008?

Their incomes stopped growing, and they blamed the people in charge.

They watched banks get rescued while they lost homes and jobs.

Immigration and cultural change made them feel they were losing status.

Spending cuts after the crisis hit the towns that depended on public money.

Which of these would have mattered without the crisis?

Timing: 19–22 minutes. Take three or four answers before revealing the list, and write each claim on the board in the room’s words. Keep the board for the takeaways.

[Sources] - Wolf (2023), pp. 99–110.

What did the crisis cost households?

Timing: 22–22 minutes.

Output per person stayed below its precrisis trend

World Bank, World Development Indicators, 2026: GDP per capita, constant dollars; trend fitted to 1990–2007.

Each year below the precrisis trend adds to the output these economies lost.

Wolf calculates that the U.K.’s loss exceeds what either world war or the Great Depression caused.

These economies never made up the output lost after 2008, and later shocks widened the gap.

Timing: 22–25 minutes.

  • Chart, percent below the 1990–2007 trend in 2025 (instructor’s calculation from World Bank data): United Kingdom 35, Spain 30, Canada 27, Italy 23, France 19, United States 16, Germany 8, Japan 2. Trend growth 1990–2007: U.K. 2.7, Spain 2.4, U.S. 2.2, Canada 2.1, France 1.7, Italy and Germany 1.4, Japan 0.9 percent a year.
  • Wolf’s figures for 2018 (Conference Board data): Spain 24, U.K. and Italy 22, U.S. and Canada 17, France 13, Japan 7 percent below trend; Germany had no significant shortfall (pp. 100–101).
  • Wolf: the U.K.’s shortfall is “a substantially bigger and more permanent loss” than either world war or the Great Depression caused (p. 101).
  • Japan and Germany grew slowly before the crisis, so they had less to lose relative to trend. Canada’s 2025 figure is larger than Wolf’s 2018 figure because growth there has been weak since 2015.

[Sources] - World Bank, WDI, NY.GDP.PCAP.KD, retrieved November 5, 2026; series in instructor/2026-11-09-series.json; original drawing. Wolf (2023), pp. 100–101, Figure 21.

Most households’ market incomes stopped rising

These are incomes from wages and investments, before taxes and government transfers.

Spending cuts after 2010 were largest in the U.S. and the U.K. among the seven largest rich economies.

Economic stagnation is a long period in which most people’s real incomes barely grow.

McKinsey Global Institute, Poorer Than Their Parents?, 2016, as shown in Wolf, The Crisis of Democratic Capitalism, 2023.

Timing: 25–28 minutes.

  • Chart, percent of households with flat or falling real market incomes, 2005–14: Italy 97, U.S. 81, U.K. 70, Netherlands 70, France 63, Sweden 20, average of 25 advanced countries 65 (Wolf: “between 65 and 70 percent,” p. 102).
  • Unemployment: U.S. 4.6 percent (2007) to 9.6 (2010); eurozone 7.6 (2007) to 12.1 (2013); Italy 12.8 (2014), still 10 in 2019; Spain 26.1 (2013), still 14.1 in 2019 (pp. 102–103).
  • Wolf on expectations: rising prosperity “from generation to generation” was the purpose these societies claimed for themselves (p. 86, earlier in the chapter).

[Sources] - Wolf (2023), pp. 86, 102–103, Figure 22, citing McKinsey Global Institute (2016); series in instructor/2026-11-09-series.json; original drawing.

Broken expectations

U.S. unemployment fell back within a few years, while most households’ incomes stayed flat. Why might stagnant incomes still anger voters?

Does anger follow the level of income, or the broken expectation that it would keep rising?

Timing: 28–32 minutes.

Answer key:

  • Wolf: people judge their lives against a “reference narrative” of realistic expectations; when it fails, the result is “disappointment, fear, and anger” (p. 85, earlier in the chapter).
  • Status anxiety: those a few rungs up the ladder, with status to defend, are most prone to it (pp. 84–85).
  • The losses cumulate: each year below trend is lost income, even after unemployment falls (p. 101).
  • Spending cuts after 2010 added to the loss; the structural tightening was largest in the U.S. and U.K. among the G7 (p. 103).

[Sources] - Wolf (2023), pp. 84–85, 101, 103.

Why did the crisis cost so much trust?

Timing: 32–32 minutes.

Banks were rescued while families lost homes

David Valdez, HUD, Paulson and Jackson at a House hearing, 2007 · Wikimedia Commons, public domain

In October 2008 Congress authorized up to $700 billion to rescue failing firms.

About 4.8 million homes were lost to foreclosure by 2013, and only one bank executive went to prison.

A corporate bailout is a government rescue that uses public money or guarantees to keep a failing firm alive.

Timing: 32–35 minutes.

  • Wolf: the public saw “the resources of the state used to rescue both banks and bankers,” while they suffered foreclosure, unemployment, stagnant wages, and austerity; “essentially nobody (or nobody of any importance) was punished” (p. 104).
  • TARP: $700 billion authorized October 3, 2008 (Emergency Economic Stabilization Act); cut to $475 billion by Dodd-Frank in 2010; about $444 billion disbursed (CRS; CBO).
  • Foreclosures: about 4.8 million completed from September 2008 to the end of 2013, against roughly 250,000 a year before the crisis (CoreLogic, January 2014).
  • Prison: Kareem Serageldin of Credit Suisse, 30 months, “the only Wall Street executive sent to jail for his part in the financial crisis” (ProPublica, April 30, 2014).
  • Photograph: Henry Paulson (left) and Alphonso Jackson before a House hearing on the mortgage crisis, September 20, 2007, a year before the rescue.

[Sources] - Wolf (2023), p. 104. CRS R41427 (June 27, 2013); CBO, “Final Report on the Troubled Asset Relief Program” (April 19, 2024); CoreLogic (January 29, 2014); ProPublica (April 30, 2014). Photograph: David Valdez, U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development, September 20, 2007, via DPLA and Wikimedia Commons, public domain, resized.

Confidence in banks collapsed after 2008

Gallup, Confidence in Institutions, 2026: banks.

Voters could see that those in charge had failed, and then saw the bankers rescued.

Wolf argues that a visible failure, followed by a rescue of those blamed for it, turned disappointment into distrust.

Timing: 35–38 minutes.

  • Chart, percent with a great deal or quite a lot of confidence in banks: 60 (1979), 36 (1990), 53 (2004), 41 (2007), 32 (2008), 22 (2009), 21 (2012, the record low), 38 (2020), 28 (2026).
  • Wolf: “Most policy mistakes in economics are invisible to the bulk of the voting public,” but this one could not be missed; many came to believe the failures reflected “intellectual and moral corruption” among decision-makers (p. 104).

[Sources] - Gallup, Confidence in Institutions, retrieved November 5, 2026; series in instructor/2026-11-09-series.json; original drawing. Wolf (2023), p. 104.

The rescue that made money

The Treasury got back more from the banks it rescued than it put in, while help for homeowners cost $31 billion. Why did the bank rescue still cost so much trust?

Is a bailout judged by what it costs or by whom it protects?

Timing: 38–42 minutes.

Answer key:

  • CBO (April 2024): TARP’s total net cost was $31 billion; financial institutions including AIG returned a net gain of $9 billion; credit-market programs a net gain of $3 billion; autos cost $12 billion; mortgage and housing programs cost $31 billion. Treasury’s bank support programs disbursed $245 billion and returned $276 billion.
  • Wolf’s reasons: the public saw bankers, the “architects” of the disaster, rescued while they lost homes and jobs, and saw no one important punished (p. 104).
  • The rescue protected creditors, shareholders who were not wiped out, and executives’ jobs; homeowners received a smaller and slower program. Fairness, not the budget, decided the verdict.

[Sources] - CBO, “Final Report on the Troubled Asset Relief Program,” April 19, 2024; Treasury Office of Financial Stability, FY2023 budget document; Wolf (2023), p. 104.

Trust in the federal government has stayed low

Pew Research Center, Public Trust in Government: 1958–2025, 2025; 2008 is the average of three polls.

Trust in the federal government fell long before 2008, and the crisis kept it near its lowest levels.

Democratic capitalism pairs a market economy with elected government, and each depends on citizens’ trust.

Timing: 42–45 minutes.

  • Chart, polls compiled by Pew: 73 (1958), 77 (1964), 36 (1974), 25 (1980), 44 (1984), 60 (October 2001, after September 11; 31 in January 2001), 31 (2007), about 25 (2008: the average of three autumn polls, 17 CBS/New York Times, 31 National Election Studies, 26 CNN), 22 (2010), 19 (2015), 17 (2019), 16 (2023), 22 (2024), 17 (September 2025). Pew’s own moving average for 2008 is 24 to 25.
  • Wolf’s chapter opens: trust in democratic institutions, the global market economy, and elites “has faded over recent decades,” shown in protectionism, hostility toward immigration, and “authoritarian populism” (p. 83).
  • The definition on the key-line is the instructor’s summary of the book’s argument.

[Sources] - Pew Research Center, December 4, 2025; series in instructor/2026-11-09-series.json; original drawing. Wolf (2023), p. 83.

In 2011 protesters camped near Wall Street and said they spoke for the 99 percent.

Timing: 45–46 minutes.

  • Occupy Wall Street began in Zuccotti Park on September 17, 2011.
  • Wolf, earlier in the chapter: from 1993 to 2015 the top 1 percent captured 52 percent of the increase in U.S. real pretax incomes (p. 91).
  • Photograph: a speaker at Occupy Wall Street, New York, 2011.

[Sources] - Wolf (2023), p. 91. Background photograph: David Shankbone, Free Speakout, Occupy Wall Street, 2011, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 3.0, resized.

Why did the backlash come after 2008?

Timing: 46–46 minutes.

The foreign-born share grew less in the U.S.

Political scientists Inglehart and Norris call populism a cultural backlash against social change.

Wolf replies that those changes ran for decades, so they cannot explain why the backlash came now.

Immigration rose less in the U.S., yet it became far more political there after the crisis.

World Bank, World Development Indicators, 2026: international migrant stock, from UN DESA.

Timing: 46–49 minutes.

  • Chart, foreign-born share of the population, 2000 and 2015, with change in points: New Zealand 17.8 to 24.5 (+6.7); U.K. 8.0 to 13.9 (+5.9); Australia 22.9 to 28.1 (+5.2); Canada 17.9 to 22.4 (+4.5); Germany 12.7 to 15.4 (+2.7); U.S. 12.4 to 14.7 (+2.3).
  • Wolf: the increase in the foreign-born share was “strikingly low in the US after 2000” and the share “modest” compared with Australia, Canada, and New Zealand (p. 109). Immigration from the new Commonwealth began in the 1950s; Enoch Powell’s speech was April 20, 1968 (p. 109).
  • Inglehart and Norris (2016): “It would be a mistake to attribute the rise of populism directly to economic inequality alone” (p. 107). Kaufmann goes further: right-wing populism “has little to do with economics” (p. 107).
  • Wolf’s reply: “The crucial difficulty with primarily cultural explanations is that they fail to provide an answer to the obvious question: Why now?” (p. 107).

[Sources] - World Bank, WDI, SM.POP.TOTL.ZS, retrieved November 5, 2026; series in instructor/2026-11-09-series.json; original drawing. Wolf (2023), pp. 107–109.

Financial crises

A study of elections from 1870 to 2014 finds that far-right parties’ vote share rises by about 30 percent of its precrisis level after financial crises, far more than after ordinary recessions. Why would a banking crisis matter more?

What can voters see in a banking crisis that they cannot see in an ordinary recession?

Timing: 49–53 minutes.

Answer key:

  • Funke, Schularick, and Trebesch (2016), 20 advanced economies, more than 800 elections, 1870–2014. Abstract: “On average, far-right parties increase their vote share by 30% after a financial crisis”; the rise is relative to the precrisis share (not percentage points) over five years. Wolf: “an increase in their vote shares of about 30 percent relative to their pre-crisis level in the five years following a systemic financial crisis” (p. 108), and the effects “are much more pronounced in financial crises” than in other recessions (p. 109).
  • Wolf: financial crises “are visible to the public and so clearly the fault of certain specific elite institutions and people” (p. 109). Governing also becomes harder after them (p. 109).
  • The rescue is visible too: the state pays for the mistakes of the rich while ordinary people pay through jobs, homes, and spending cuts (p. 104).

[Sources] - Manuel Funke, Moritz Schularick, and Christoph Trebesch, “Going to Extremes: Politics after Financial Crises, 1870–2014,” European Economic Review 88 (2016): 227–260; Wolf (2023), pp. 104, 108–109.

Can a bank rescue keep public trust?

Timing: 53–53 minutes.

Attach one condition to a bank rescue

  1. Choose one condition for rescuing the banks in October 2008: wipe out shareholders, cap and claw back executives’ pay, pair the rescue with mortgage relief for homeowners, or prosecute executives who broke the law.
  2. Diagnose which cause of distrust in Wolf it would address, citing one passage.
  3. Name one risk it creates for the rescue itself.
  4. Defend your choice to the person next to you.

15 minutes · Individual, then pairs · Reading permitted

Timing: 53–68 minutes. Ten minutes alone, five in pairs. A choice cannot be “all four.”

Answer key:

  • Wiping out shareholders answers the sense that the rich were spared, but may scare away private capital and make other banks harder to save.
  • Clawing back pay answers “nobody … was punished” (p. 104), but executives may leave or fight in court; the sums are small next to the losses.
  • Mortgage relief answers the contrast between rescued banks and foreclosed families (p. 104); it is slow and costly to deliver, and the actual housing programs cost $31 billion (CBO).
  • Prosecution answers the absence of punishment, but cases take years and need proof of crimes, not bad judgment; one Wall Street executive went to prison (ProPublica).

[Sources] - Wolf (2023), p. 104; CBO (April 19, 2024); ProPublica (April 30, 2014).

Report out

Which condition would have done most to keep the public’s trust, and what would it have risked?

Can a rescue stop a panic and still look fair to the public?

Timing: 68–72 minutes. Tally the four choices aloud, then ask one pair per choice for its risk. Write two columns on the board, trust gained and risk taken.

Closing discussion

Wolf wrote in 2022 that COVID and the war in Ukraine left people looking to governments for help. In 2026 fuel and fertilizer prices have jumped after the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. What would Wolf expect this to do to politics?

Which matters more for trust: how large the shock is, or who seems to pay for it?

Timing: 72–83 minutes. Open discussion. Cold-call three or four students on their IB Voice answers first.

  • Wolf on COVID and the war in Ukraine: people “looked to help from governments,” and “there was only so much governments could do” (p. 105).
  • Expected answers: a shock seen as an act of nature or of a foreign government may not destroy trust the way 2008 did (Wolf contrasts COVID, viewed “as an act of God,” p. 105); what matters is whether the response looks fair. 2026 figures if asked: Brent averaged about $125 a barrel in October (EIA); U.S. retail diesel set a record of $6.53 a gallon on September 21 (EIA); world urea peaked at $857 a ton in April, up from $472 in February (World Bank).

[Sources] - Wolf (2023), p. 105.

Module 7 takeaways

How does globalization produce political backlash?

Trade and offshoring raise national income, but the losses fall on particular workers.

Those losses spread through the places the workers live, long after the factory closes.

After 2008 most households’ incomes stalled for years.

The bank rescue, seen as saving those who caused the crisis, turned disappointment into distrust of elites.

That distrust weakened democratic capitalism, as the young turned from capitalism and others turned to populists.

Timing: 83–90 minutes. Before each click, ask the room for its answer, then reveal the line. Line one is November 2 (Boo, Chennai and the United States), line two is November 4 (Cameron County and Broz, Frieden, and Weymouth), lines three to five are today. Return to the opening puzzle with the last line: Wolf explains why trust fell after 2008; the Gallup data show that among the young and Democrats the response was to think less of capitalism, while Wolf’s chapter follows the voters who turned to right-wing populists (pp. 114–115, outside the assigned pages, explains why the right gained more). Return to the board: the first hypothesis is the long trend; the second and fourth are the crisis and its aftermath; the third is the cultural explanation Wolf answers with “Why now?” End in open discussion on the last line.

  • Wednesday, November 11, opens Module 8, how shocks travel through global business: Peter S. Goodman, How the World Ran Out of Everything, chs. 3, 10, and 18.

[Sources] - Wolf (2023), pp. 99–110; Boo (2004); Broz, Frieden, and Weymouth (2021).
